2:165.en: And [yet], among the people are those who take other than Allah as equals [to Him]. They love them as they [should] love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah. And if only they who have wronged would consider [that] when they see the punishment, [they will be certain] that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is severe in punishment

5:54.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ مَن يَرۡتَدَّ مِنكُمۡ عَن دِينِهِۦ فَسَوۡفَ يَأۡتِي ٱللَّهُ بِقَوۡمࣲ يُحِبُّهُمۡ وَيُحِبُّونَهُۥٓ أَذِلَّةٍ عَلَى ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ أَعِزَّةٍ عَلَى ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ يُجَٰهِدُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَلَا يَخَافُونَ لَوۡمَةَ لَآئِمࣲۚ ذَٰلِكَ فَضۡلُ ٱللَّهِ يُؤۡتِيهِ مَن يَشَآءُۚ وَٱللَّهُ وَٰسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ
5:54.en: O you who have believed, whoever of you should revert from his religion - Allah will bring forth [in place of them] a people He will love and who will love Him [who are] humble toward the believers, powerful against the disbelievers; they strive in the cause of Allah and do not fear the blame of a critic. That is the favor of Allah; He bestows it upon whom He wills. And Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing

58:22.ar: لَّا تَجِدُ قَوۡمࣰ ا يُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡيَوۡمِ ٱلۡأٓخِرِ يُوَآدُّونَ مَنۡ حَآدَّ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ وَلَوۡ كَانُوٓاْ ءَابَآءَهُمۡ أَوۡ أَبۡنَآءَهُمۡ أَوۡ إِخۡوَٰنَهُمۡ أَوۡ عَشِيرَتَهُمۡۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ كَتَبَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ ٱلۡإِيمَٰنَ وَأَيَّدَهُم بِرُوحࣲ مِّنۡهُۖ وَيُدۡخِلُهُمۡ جَنَّٰتࣲ تَجۡرِي مِن تَحۡتِهَا ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُ خَٰلِدِينَ فِيهَاۚ رَضِيَ ٱللَّهُ عَنۡهُمۡ وَرَضُواْ عَنۡهُۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ حِزۡبُ ٱللَّهِۚ أَلَآ إِنَّ حِزۡبَ ٱللَّهِ هُمُ ٱلۡمُفۡلِحُونَ
58:22.en: You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day having affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their kindred. Those - He has decreed within their hearts faith and supported them with spirit from Him. And We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they abide eternally. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him - those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah - they are the successful

16:6.ar: وَلَكُمۡ فِيهَا جَمَالٌ حِينَ تُرِيحُونَ وَحِينَ تَسۡرَحُونَ
16:6.en: And for you in them is [the enjoyment of] beauty when you bring them in [for the evening] and when you send them out [to pasture]

16:7.ar: وَتَحۡمِلُ أَثۡقَالَكُمۡ إِلَىٰ بَلَدࣲ لَّمۡ تَكُونُواْ بَٰلِغِيهِ إِلَّا بِشِقِّ ٱلۡأَنفُسِۚ إِنَّ رَبَّكُمۡ لَرَءُوفࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
16:7.en: And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with difficulty to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful

16:8.ar: وَٱلۡخَيۡلَ وَٱلۡبِغَالَ وَٱلۡحَمِيرَ لِتَرۡكَبُوهَا وَزِينَةࣰۚ وَيَخۡلُقُ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
16:8.en: And [He created] the horses, mules and donkeys for you to ride and [as] adornment. And He creates that which you do not know

7:31.ar: ۞يَٰبَنِيٓ ءَادَمَ خُذُواْ زِينَتَكُمۡ عِندَ كُلِّ مَسۡجِدࣲ وَكُلُواْ وَٱشۡرَبُواْ وَلَا تُسۡرِفُوٓاْۚ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلۡمُسۡرِفِينَ
7:31.en: O children of Adam, take your adornment at every masjid, and eat and drink, but be not excessive. Indeed, He likes not those who commit excess

9:24.ar: قُلۡ إِن كَانَ ءَابَآؤُكُمۡ وَأَبۡنَآؤُكُمۡ وَإِخۡوَٰنُكُمۡ وَأَزۡوَٰجُكُمۡ وَعَشِيرَتُكُمۡ وَأَمۡوَٰلٌ ٱقۡتَرَفۡتُمُوهَا وَتِجَٰرَةࣱ تَخۡشَوۡنَ كَسَادَهَا وَمَسَٰكِنُ تَرۡضَوۡنَهَآ أَحَبَّ إِلَيۡكُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ وَجِهَادࣲ فِي سَبِيلِهِۦ فَتَرَبَّصُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَأۡتِيَ ٱللَّهُ بِأَمۡرِهِۦۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
9:24.en: Say, [O Muhammad], "If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, your relatives, wealth which you have obtained, commerce wherein you fear decline, and dwellings with which you are pleased are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and jihad in His cause, then wait until Allah executes His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people

15:47.ar: وَنَزَعۡنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنۡ غِلٍّ إِخۡوَٰنًا عَلَىٰ سُرُرࣲ مُّتَقَٰبِلِينَ
15:47.en: And We will remove whatever is in their breasts of resentment, [so they will be] brothers, on thrones facing each other

eaTI4MgKJWQ.speaker: adnan
eaTI4MgKJWQ.speaker_note: the sheikh's own Values of Islam series, refers back to his sessions of the previous two mornings
eaTI4MgKJWQ.title: The Values of Islam: Love (al-Hubb) and Beauty (al-Jamal)
eaTI4MgKJWQ.one_line: Love and beauty are Islam's highest ideals, but they can only grow in a society that first secures justice, righteousness and core ethics.
eaTI4MgKJWQ.summary: Closing his series on the values of Islam, the sheikh presents love and beauty as high-order ideals that only make sense once a society has its core ethics in place. Ideals without the foundation become hollow, and young people sense the hypocrisy. He asks how love can exist where oppression reigns, using the verse that Allah may one day place love between believers and their enemies, which presupposes that the oppression ends first. He separates genuine love from selfish attachment that uses people for benefit, defining love as seeing another person as an extension of yourself. Because love makes a person vulnerable, it needs a just society to protect it, and he offers his own theory that all of Islam's ethics exist so that people can love safely. He traces love through the Quran and hadith, then turns to beauty: Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, yet beautifying houses, masjids or cities is pointless when the interior is full of injustice. He ends with Ali grieving over Talhah in the middle of a battle, and with the early Muslims, who had little wealth but carried the faith across the world because they loved. He asks the community to secure the basics so love and beauty can flourish.

outline.heading: High ideals need a foundation of core ethics
outline.gist: Ideals without basic ethics are fake and backfire, because young people notice the inconsistency and question the whole system.

outline.heading: Build upward: Islam as a moral code
outline.gist: Priorities matter; without the moral code, faith becomes a skeleton and prayer becomes mechanical movement.

outline.heading: Can love exist without justice?
outline.gist: A society that preaches love while full of oppression makes love impossible; he means love between people, not love of Allah.

outline.heading: Love toward enemies only after oppression ends (60:7)
outline.gist: The verse hopes for love with former enemies, but only once their aggression, land theft and persecution are removed.

outline.heading: Fish love: selfish love is not love
outline.gist: Loving someone for benefit or to boost your ego is using them, a kind of non-financial usury.

outline.heading: Love as seeing someone as an extension of yourself
outline.gist: You protect and care for the beloved as you would your own eye or heart.

outline.heading: Love makes you vulnerable
outline.gist: In an unjust society people who love get abused, and after being burnt once or twice they stop loving.

outline.heading: His theory: ethics exist so people can love safely
outline.gist: All of Islam's ethics serve to let people be vulnerable and express love while protected.

outline.heading: Loving for your brother what you love for yourself
outline.gist: The hadith makes faith depend on treating others as yourself.

outline.heading: Love throughout the Quran and Sunnah
outline.gist: Believers love Allah most, Allah loves a people who love Him, the sweetness of faith, hatred as love of the opposite, and telling your brother you love him.

outline.heading: Loving people simply as Allah's creation
outline.gist: Love without ulterior motive keeps society alive and could even reach enemies once wrongs are fixed.

outline.heading: Beauty in the Quran: livestock and riding animals (16:6-8)
outline.gist: Allah points out the beauty in animals and says He is beautiful and loves beauty.

outline.heading: Beautiful exterior, rotten interior
outline.gist: A perfect house without love is pointless; Allah asks for adornment at the masjid and beautiful recitation, but beauty must sit on substance.

outline.heading: A painted city full of oppression
outline.gist: Beautifying streets while injustice remains is empty; people feeling valued matters more than nice carpets.

outline.heading: Allah as the source of all beauty
outline.gist: The highest people in Jannah want nothing but their appointments to see Allah's face, the source of all beauty.

outline.heading: What Muslims miss when core ethics are neglected
outline.gist: Without righteousness and justice we lose the ability to love genuinely and appreciate beauty, and life becomes dull.

outline.heading: Love is felt in everything, and Ramadan is a search for it
outline.gist: Love is felt even in food and small gestures; in Ramadan we are waiting for a moment of loving Allah and feeling His love.

outline.heading: No lasting love or beauty without the basics
outline.gist: Without the core values the experience is artificial; with them every leaf and star becomes a sign of Allah's beauty.

outline.heading: If family and wealth are dearer than Allah (9:24)
outline.gist: Putting anything above love of Allah and His Messenger means missing the most important thing.

outline.heading: Early Muslims: simple means, deep love
outline.gist: They had plain masjids but felt and expressed love and beauty, and kept their love even through bitter disagreements.

outline.heading: Ali and Talhah at the battle
outline.gist: Ali weeps over the dying Talhah, hopes they will be brothers in Jannah with rancour removed, and buries him, though they fought on opposite sides.

outline.heading: A loveless community and a loveless marriage
outline.gist: Without love people tire of their faith and relationships; a marriage needs justice and fair treatment before love can grow.

outline.heading: Series recap: the society Islam aims for
outline.gist: Forgiveness, chivalry, generosity, love and beauty grow from protected basics; the Sahaba carried the faith out of love for the Prophet.

themes.label: Love: of Allah, the Prophet, and one another
themes.note: Defines genuine love as seeing others as an extension of oneself and argues it needs a just society to survive.

themes.label: Values, principles and ethics as a system
themes.note: High ideals sit on core ethics; without the base they are hollow and push the young away.

themes.label: Priorities in the deen: fundamentals before details
themes.note: Build from the basics upward and know what can and cannot be dropped.

themes.label: Justice and refusing oppression
themes.note: Love is impossible where oppression reigns; even love toward enemies requires their aggression to end first.

themes.label: Beauty (jamal) and appreciating Allah's creation
themes.note: Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, but outward beautification is pointless when the inside is unjust.

themes.label: The companions and the early generations
themes.note: The Sahaba had little but loved deeply, shown in Ali grieving over Talhah mid-battle.

themes.label: Marriage and the relationship between spouses
themes.note: Spouses cannot find love without fixing mistreatment and bringing fairness first.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: Seeing Allah's face is the greatest delight of the highest ranks of Jannah.

quran.point: Allah may place love between believers and former enemies, once oppression is removed.
Others love rivals as they should love Allah, but believers are stronger in love for Allah.
Allah brings a people whom He loves and who love Him.
True believers do not love those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.
Beauty in livestock and riding animals as a sign Allah wants us to notice.
Take your adornment at every masjid.
Warning to those who love family, trade and homes more than Allah, His Messenger and striving in His way.
Ali hopes he and Talhah will be among those whose rancour is removed, brothers on couches in Jannah.

hadith.gist: Those who love one another for Allah's sake will be on pulpits of light that others envy.
None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
Three qualities give the sweetness of faith: loving Allah and His Messenger most, loving others only for Allah, and hating to return to disbelief.
If you love your brother, tell him.
Allah is beautiful and loves beauty.
Beautify the Quran with your voices; the best voice is one that makes you think the reciter fears Allah.
The people of the highest rank in Jannah look upon Allah's face morning and evening.

maxims: Love is seeing someone as an extension of yourself
Fish love is not love
Selfish love is non-financial riba
Hatred is just loving the opposite thing
All of Islam's ethics exist so we can love safely

stories.who: Ali ibn Abi Talib and Talhah ibn Ubaydullah
stories.point: Even on opposite sides of a battle, the companions never lost their love for one another.

contemporary: A government beautifying streets and removing graffiti while injustice and inequality remain
takeaways: Secure the basics of justice, righteousness and fair treatment before speaking of higher ideals.
Love people for Allah's sake and as His creation, not for what they give you.
Tell the people you love that you love them.
Notice and appreciate beauty in creation as a sign of Allah's beauty.
In a marriage or community, repair mistreatment first so love can grow.

24:22.ar: وَلَا يَأۡتَلِ أُوْلُواْ ٱلۡفَضۡلِ مِنكُمۡ وَٱلسَّعَةِ أَن يُؤۡتُوٓاْ أُوْلِي ٱلۡقُرۡبَىٰ وَٱلۡمَسَٰكِينَ وَٱلۡمُهَٰجِرِينَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِۖ وَلۡيَعۡفُواْ وَلۡيَصۡفَحُوٓاْۗ أَلَا تُحِبُّونَ أَن يَغۡفِرَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمٌ
24:22.en: And let not those of virtue among you and wealth swear not to give [aid] to their relatives and the needy and the emigrants for the cause of Allah, and let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful

xMqwsBv8UB4.speaker: adnan
xMqwsBv8UB4.speaker_note: gives both reminders between rakaat on the 27th night in his usual English style; part of his Ramadan 2026 series
xMqwsBv8UB4.title: Ramadan 2026, Night 27: Seventh Night of Tahajjud
xMqwsBv8UB4.one_line: On the 27th night: ask Allah for pardon that erases sins completely, and earn it by pardoning those who wronged you.
xMqwsBv8UB4.summary: The 27th night reminders are both about pardon. In the first he says the night is about your own ability to pardon others: the Prophet taught Aisha to ask Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon on this night, and the verse revealed about Abu Bakr asks believers to pardon and overlook if they want Allah to forgive them. He cites the words found on the Prophet's sword, give to whoever deprives you, reconnect with whoever cuts you off, pardon whoever wrongs you and be good to whoever harms you, as the code the Prophet lived by, and Umar's public release of everyone from any claim he had on them, reasoning that Allah will not be outdone by His servants. In the second reminder he separates forgiveness from pardon: a forgiven sin stays in your book, stamped forgiven, while a pardoned sin is gone as if it never happened. He paints a scene of searching your book on the Day of Judgement for a sin you feared and never finding it, because Allah erased it from the record, from the angels and from everyone who saw it. He asks people to spend the coming minutes finding the strength to pardon someone, because it is impossible to pardon and not be pardoned.

outline.heading: Opening
Interlude
Tonight is about pardoning, and the dua taught to Aisha
outline.gist: The 27th night is about your ability to pardon those around you; the Prophet taught Aisha to ask Allah, who loves to pardon, to pardon her on this night.

outline.heading: Pardon so that Allah forgives you
outline.gist: The verse revealed about Abu Bakr: let them pardon and overlook; do you not love that Allah should forgive you?

outline.heading: The code written on the Prophet's sword
outline.gist: Ali found on the hilt of the Prophet's sword: give to whoever deprives you, reconnect with whoever cuts you off, pardon whoever wrongs you, be good to whoever harms you. This is what he lived by.

outline.heading: Umar releases everyone from their debts to him
outline.gist: Umar declared that people were free of any claim he had on them and asked the same of them, trusting that Allah would not fail to pardon when His servants pardon.

outline.heading: Find a way to pardon and never bring it up again
outline.gist: If you dig deep enough to pardon someone who wronged you, Allah will pardon you; see them in a light that lets you forgive, and never hold it against them or speak of it again.

outline.heading: Interlude
Sins concealed in this world, forgiven on that Day
outline.gist: On the Day of Judgement a believer finds sins he is not proud of in his book, and Allah tells him He concealed them in the world and forgives them today.

outline.heading: Forgiveness versus pardon, and why pardon belongs to this night
outline.gist: A forgiven sin is still documented in the book; pardon is of a higher order and so rare that the Prophet tied asking for it to the best night of the year.

outline.heading: Searching your book for a pardoned sin
outline.gist: An imagined scene: you flip through your book for the date of a sin you feared, cannot find it, ask the person involved and the recording angels, and it never comes up before Allah.

outline.heading: Allah erases it from every memory
outline.gist: Allah tells you that on the 27th night of Ramadan 2026 you asked for pardon and He erased the sin from your book and from the memory of the angels, witnesses and those affected; soon you forget it too.

outline.heading: Someone here has to pardon
outline.gist: He needs at least one person in the room to find the strength to pardon someone who wronged or oppressed them, however hard it is.

outline.heading: You cannot outdo Allah in generosity
outline.gist: Use the coming minutes to forgive those who wronged you: it is impossible to pardon and not be pardoned, and forgiving lifts a burden off you.

outline.heading: Interlude
Outro

themes.label: Mercy, forgiveness and pardoning people
themes.note: Pardoning those who wronged you is the way to Allah's pardon, modelled by the Prophet's code, Abu Bakr and Umar.

themes.label: Mercy, forgiveness and pardoning people
themes.note: A direct call for someone in the room to pardon tonight, since Allah cannot be outdone in generosity.

themes.label: The Names and Attributes of Allah
themes.note: Allah as Al-Afuww: pardon erases a sin entirely, beyond forgiveness that leaves it recorded.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: The book of deeds on the Day of Judgement and what a pardoned sin looks like there.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: The four lines on his sword were the principles he lived by.

themes.label: Ramadan: preparation, fasting, making the most of it
themes.note: Asking for pardon is tied to Laylat al-Qadr because pardon is so rare and precious.

quran.point: Let them pardon and overlook; do you not love that Allah should forgive you? Revealed about Abu Bakr.

hadith.gist: Aisha asked what to say if she found Laylat al-Qadr; the Prophet taught her: O Allah, You are Pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me.
Ali found written on the hilt of the Prophet's sword: give to whoever deprives you, keep ties with whoever cuts you off, pardon whoever wrongs you, and be good to whoever harms you.
Allah draws the believer close on the Day of Judgement, makes him acknowledge his sins, then says He concealed them in the world and forgives them today.

maxims: Tonight is all about forgiveness
Pardon means it is as if you never did it
It is impossible that you pardon and Allah does not
You cannot be more generous than the Generous One

stories.who: Abu Bakr
stories.point: The verse urging believers to pardon and overlook was revealed about him: pardoning those who wrong you invites Allah's forgiveness.

stories.who: Umar ibn al-Khattab
stories.point: He publicly released people from any claim he had on them, confident that Allah pardons those who pardon.

stories.who: A believer searching his book on the Day of Judgement
stories.point: A sin Allah has pardoned cannot be found anywhere, not in the book and not in anyone's memory.

takeaways: On Laylat al-Qadr, ask Allah again and again for pardon with the dua taught to Aisha.
Pick someone who wronged you and pardon them tonight, then never bring it up again.
Live by the Prophet's code: give to those who deprive you, reconnect with those who cut you off, pardon and be good to those who harm you.
Aim for pardon that erases sins, not only forgiveness that leaves them on record.

78:1.en: About what are they asking one another

78:3.en: That over which they are in disagreement

78:4.en: No! They are going to know

78:5.en: Then, no! They are going to know

78:6.en: Have We not made the earth a resting place

78:8.en: And We created you in pairs

78:9.en: And made your sleep [a means for] rest

78:10.en: And made the night as clothing

78:11.en: And made the day for livelihood

78:12.ar: وَبَنَيۡنَا فَوۡقَكُمۡ سَبۡعࣰ ا شِدَادࣰ ا
78:12.en: And constructed above you seven strong [heavens]

78:14.ar: وَأَنزَلۡنَا مِنَ ٱلۡمُعۡصِرَٰتِ مَآءࣰ ثَجَّاجࣰ ا
78:14.en: And sent down, from the rain clouds, pouring water

78:15.ar: لِّنُخۡرِجَ بِهِۦ حَبࣰّ ا وَنَبَاتࣰ ا
78:15.en: That We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation

78:17.ar: إِنَّ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡفَصۡلِ كَانَ مِيقَٰتࣰ ا
78:17.en: Indeed, the Day of Judgement is an appointed time

78:18.ar: يَوۡمَ يُنفَخُ فِي ٱلصُّورِ فَتَأۡتُونَ أَفۡوَاجࣰ ا
78:18.en: The Day the Horn is blown and you will come forth in multitudes

78:19.en: And the heaven is opened and will become gateways

78:20.en: And the mountains are removed and will be [but] a mirage

78:21.en: Indeed, Hell has been lying in wait

78:22.en: For the transgressors, a place of return

78:23.en: In which they will remain for ages [unending]

78:24.ar: لَّا يَذُوقُونَ فِيهَا بَرۡدࣰ ا وَلَا شَرَابًا
78:24.en: They will not taste therein [any] coolness or drink

78:27.ar: إِنَّهُمۡ كَانُواْ لَا يَرۡجُونَ حِسَابࣰ ا
78:27.en: Indeed, they were not expecting an account

78:28.en: And denied Our verses with [emphatic] denial

78:29.en: But all things We have enumerated in writing

78:30.en: So taste [the penalty], and never will We increase you except in torment

78:31.en: Indeed, for the righteous is attainment

78:35.ar: لَّا يَسۡمَعُونَ فِيهَا لَغۡوࣰ ا وَلَا كِذَّٰبࣰ ا
78:35.en: No ill speech will they hear therein or any falsehood

r_9x2DpW0_E.speaker: adnan
r_9x2DpW0_E.speaker_note: final night of his A Juz A Day series; welcomes viewers and teaches throughout in his own voice
r_9x2DpW0_E.title: A Juz A Day: 30th Juz - A Beautiful Ending
r_9x2DpW0_E.one_line: A thematic tour of Juz Amma: tawhid, the Prophet's duty to convey, belief in the unseen, faith as good deeds of every kind, and fickle human nature.
r_9x2DpW0_E.summary: For the final night he takes the 30th juz by theme rather than in order, since its short, rhythmic Makkan surahs were built to reach an audience that refused to listen. Tawhid comes first: Al-Ikhlas affirms Allah's unique oneness, which he says we cheapen by treating it as a filler surah, while Al-Kafirun purges false belief and draws clear lines. Al-Fil and Quraysh show the security Allah gave Quraysh for Ibrahim's sake, which they turned into an idol business. An-Naba, Ash-Shams and Al-Masad present proofs all around us, the inner inspiration of every soul, and a fulfilled prophecy, from which he derives three layers of accountability: fitrah, the signs, and revelation. Abasa, Al-Ala and Al-Ghashiyah teach that the Prophet's job, and ours, is the effort, not the result, which he calls liberating. On the unseen, he argues from the long odds of conception and birth to resurrection, and explains that deeds are weighed by their difficulty and sincerity. The buried girl being questioned shows that the oppressed will get their full day in court. He closes with faith as good deeds of every kind, from patience and gratitude to compassion and honest trade, and with the ungrateful human contrasted with the loyal charging horse.

outline.heading: Opening
Short, rhythmic surahs for an audience refusing to listen
outline.gist: The juz runs from An-Naba to An-Nas; nearly all are Makkan, made short and impactful so the message could not be missed, and it holds the first revelation and the last complete surah.

outline.heading: Surahs of special virtue
outline.gist: Narrations describe some surahs as a quarter or a third of the Quran, and the Prophet recited the last three after every prayer and before sleep.

outline.heading: The major themes and a thematic approach
outline.gist: Tawhid, the Prophet's duty to deliver, belief in the unseen, faith as good deeds, and human nature turned from fickle to resolute; he will move by theme to touch every surah.

outline.heading: Al-Ikhlas: Allah the One, the Self-Sufficient
outline.gist: Ahad means unlike any; everyone depends on Him and He on no one; He neither begets nor was begotten and nothing is comparable to Him.

outline.heading: Not a filler surah
outline.gist: We often recite Al-Ikhlas as a default when nothing else comes to mind, which takes away from the gravity of its message.

outline.heading: Al-Kafirun with Al-Ikhlas: purge and affirm
outline.gist: The Prophet praised a man who recited both and paired them in the sunnah prayers, since true belief needs false beliefs removed and the truth affirmed.

outline.heading: To you your religion: drawing the lines
outline.gist: The surah separates the two ways clearly: they made their choice, and ours is to worship Allah alone.

outline.heading: Interlude
Al-Fil: Abraha's army and the birds
outline.gist: Abraha marched to destroy the Kaaba; Abdul Muttalib said the House has a Lord who will protect it, the elephants refused to move and the birds pelted the army.

outline.heading: Quraysh: security as a favour to be repaid with worship
outline.gist: The event made Quraysh untouchable and their caravans safe in a lawless land, yet they added idols to the Kaaba for trade; they are told to worship the Lord of the House instead of making it a business.

outline.heading: An-Naba: the earth, the mountains and the systems of life
outline.gist: Instead of describing the Judgment directly, Allah turns attention to the smoothed earth, stabilizing mountains, pairs, sleep as rest, night as cover and day for livelihood.

outline.heading: Squeezed clouds and the appointed day of decision
outline.gist: The seven heavens, the blazing lamp and rain pressed from clouds feed us; the same Lord who set all this up will remove it and gather us.

outline.heading: Hell lying in wait and an ironclad record
outline.gist: Those who enjoyed the systems Allah made but never feared reckoning are convicted by a complete record and only increased in torment.

outline.heading: The ultimate success of the righteous
outline.gist: Gardens, vineyards, companions and a full cup, with no idle or lying talk: a fitting gift from their Lord.

outline.heading: The day of truth and the wish to be dust
outline.gist: No one speaks without permission; every person sees what their hands sent ahead, and the disbeliever wishes he had never existed.

outline.heading: Ash-Shams: oaths that move the heart
outline.gist: The rhythmic oaths by the sun, moon, day, night, sky, earth and soul carry a force he likens to a man who felt his heart would fly from his chest on hearing the Quran.

outline.heading: The soul inspired with its wickedness and its piety
outline.gist: Every soul knows right from wrong; the one who acts on it purifies itself and succeeds, the one who buries it fails.

outline.heading: Thamud and the camel: a sign ignored
outline.gist: Every soul seeks its Lord, especially in extremity, yet a physical sign does nothing for someone determined to suppress that instinct.

outline.heading: Three levels of accountability
outline.gist: Kufr is burying the inner seed of fitrah; above it come reflection on the signs of creation and then the revelation itself, and accountability rises with each level a person had.

outline.heading: Al-Masad: why Abu Lahab is named
outline.gist: The Quran rarely names opponents; Abu Lahab and his wife, who left obstacles at the Prophet's door, are named for their role.

outline.heading: The call at Safa and a prophecy fulfilled
outline.gist: After the people affirmed the Prophet's honesty, his uncle was first to reject him publicly, setting a precedent; the surah foretold he would never believe, and he died a disbeliever.

outline.heading: Abasa: he frowned at the blind man
outline.gist: The surah reproaches attention given to the self-satisfied over the eager seeker, then reminds humans of their origin from a drop and their return.

outline.heading: Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum and the chiefs of Quraysh
outline.gist: The Prophet hoped winning the arrogant chiefs would bring their followers; Allah told him results are not his job, only conveying to those who seek.

outline.heading: Al-Ala: remind, and do not prefer this world
outline.gist: The God-fearing heed the reminder and the wretched ignore it; we may thrive in this temporary life but not at the expense of the permanent one, a message in the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa.

outline.heading: Al-Ghashiyah: your job is the effort, not the result
outline.gist: The Prophet was only a reminder, not a controller; focusing on effort and trusting Allah for results is liberating and stress-free, while accountability is Allah's.

outline.heading: Belief in the unseen: created from a gushing fluid
outline.gist: If Allah created you the first time from a drop, He can recreate you; humans should reflect on their origin.

outline.heading: Against long odds, so resurrection is not far-fetched
outline.gist: The odds of conception and of a safe birth are small, yet each of us was created; recreating us is no harder.

outline.heading: Al-Qariah: scattered moths and fluffed wool
outline.gist: People will scatter without order and immovable mountains blow away like wool; the whole world is transformed.

outline.heading: Heavy and light scales, and the bottomless pit
outline.gist: Heavy deeds bring a pleasing life; light ones lead to a blazing fire with no limit to its depth.

outline.heading: Deeds weighed by difficulty and sincerity
outline.gist: The same act weighs differently depending on effort and sincerity, so quality matters most; struggling to learn the Quran earns more than learning it easily.

outline.heading: My brothers who believe without seeing me
outline.gist: The Prophet said those who come later and believe without seeing him will have the reward of fifty of his companions for their good deeds, because it is harder for them.

outline.heading: Al-Infitar: when the sky splits
outline.gist: Scattered stars, bursting seas and overturned graves, and every soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind.

outline.heading: Al-Inshiqaq: toiling toward your Lord
outline.gist: Life is toil toward meeting Allah; the one who knows he failed hides his left hand behind his back, having lived content and assuming he would never return.

outline.heading: At-Takwir: abandoned camels and gathered beasts
outline.gist: The most prized asset is abandoned, animals are gathered for justice, and souls are rejoined to bodies.

outline.heading: The buried girl is asked: the oppressed get their day in court
outline.gist: The victim, not the guilty perpetrator, is questioned so that full justice is served; we take solace in that while working to correct injustice now.

outline.heading: Al-Humazah: the slanderer owned by his money
outline.gist: Keeping track of money is responsible, but the one who counts it obsessively and thinks it makes him immortal is thrown into the crushing fire.

outline.heading: Al-Asr: faith is doing good deeds
outline.gist: Humanity is in loss except those who believe, do good, and urge each other to truth and steadfastness.

outline.heading: Al-Kawthar: patience and gratitude after loss
outline.gist: When the Prophet lost his son and Quraysh rejoiced, he was told he had been given abundance, to pray and sacrifice and ignore them.

outline.heading: At-Tin: the potential to be the best or the lowest
outline.gist: The oaths point to the lands of the great prophets; humans are made in the finest form and fall to the lowest unless they believe and do good.

outline.heading: Al-Balad: the steep path of compassion
outline.gist: Freeing a slave and feeding the hungry orphan or poor person, Muslim or not, is the steep path, followed by urging patience and compassion.

outline.heading: Al-Mutaffifin: business ethics
outline.gist: Those who demand full measure but give short are warned of resurrection; faith includes honest trade and turning to Allah for ease after hardship.

outline.heading: Al-Fajr: honoured in ease, humiliated in hardship
outline.gist: Even a believer can be fickle, reading blessings as honour and scarcity as humiliation; true faith thanks Allah in good and stays calm in bad.

outline.heading: Al-Adiyat: the loyal horse and the ungrateful human
outline.gist: The war horse charges to its death for a master who did not create it, while humans who owe Allah everything find the one black spot on a white canvas.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Tawhid and worship of Allah alone
themes.note: Al-Ikhlas affirms Allah's uniqueness, Al-Kafirun purges false belief, and Quraysh are told to worship the Lord of the House rather than profit from it.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: The signs of creation in An-Naba lead straight to the day of decision and the ironclad record.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: Resurrection argued from the long odds of birth, the weighing of deeds, and the scenes of the Last Day.

themes.label: Accountability before Allah and goals
themes.note: Fitrah, the signs and revelation are three layers of accountability; no one is punished without cause.

themes.label: Dawah, outreach and representing Islam
themes.note: The Prophet's job, and ours, is to convey and to give our best effort, not to secure results.

themes.label: Intention and sincerity (niyyah, ikhlas)
themes.note: Deeds are weighed by sincerity and difficulty, so later believers who struggle earn a multiplied reward.

themes.label: Justice and refusing oppression
themes.note: Questioning the buried girl shows the oppressed will get full justice; meanwhile we work against injustice now.

themes.label: Wealth, asceticism (zuhd), consumerism and money
themes.note: Managing money is responsible; being owned by it and thinking it grants permanence is destructive.

themes.label: Values, principles and ethics as a system
themes.note: Faith is belief, speech and action: patience, gratitude, compassion for all people and honest trade.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation
themes.note: Humans swing between pride and despair and fixate on the one flaw, unlike the horse loyal to its master.

hadith.gist: Certain surahs of this juz are described as equal to a quarter of the Quran, and Al-Ikhlas as equal to a third.
The Prophet recited Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas after every prayer, three times after Fajr and Maghrib, and before sleeping.
The Prophet praised a man who recited Al-Kafirun and Al-Ikhlas as one who knows his Lord, and recited these two in the sunnah prayers before Fajr.
The Prophet said he longed to meet his brothers, those who would believe in him without seeing him, and that the doer of good among them would have the reward of fifty of his companions.

maxims: Your job is the effort, not the result
Quality is what matters to Allah
Kufr is burying the seed of fitrah
The oppressed will get their day in court
Don't treat Al-Ikhlas as a filler

stories.who: Abraha and the army of the elephant
stories.point: Allah protected the Kaaba for Ibrahim's sake, and Quraysh's resulting security was a favour to be repaid with worship.

stories.who: The Prophet at Mount Safa and Abu Lahab
stories.point: His uncle's public rejection set the precedent for persecution, and the surah's prophecy that he would never believe came true.

stories.who: Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum and the chiefs of Quraysh
stories.point: The sincere seeker deserves attention over the arrogant; the results of dawah belong to Allah.

stories.who: The death of the Prophet's son
stories.point: Answered with Al-Kawthar: patience, gratitude and ignoring those who gloat.

contemporary: Treating Surah Al-Ikhlas as a default recitation in prayer
Modern medicine lowering infant mortality, set against the long natural odds of birth
takeaways: Recite Al-Ikhlas with reflection rather than as a filler, and keep the sunnah of the protective surahs after prayers and before sleep
Focus on giving your best effort in dawah and in life, and leave the results to Allah
Persist with hard deeds like learning the Quran, knowing difficulty and sincerity add weight
Show compassion to all people, feed the hungry and deal honestly in business
Meet both blessing and hardship with gratitude and calm instead of pride or despair

94sXD9O24Ys.speaker: adnan
94sXD9O24Ys.speaker_note: closing night of his Ramadan series; speaks of his own teacher and his article for the centre's publication
94sXD9O24Ys.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 29 - Quranic Themes: Outcomes
94sXD9O24Ys.one_line: Every choice has an outcome: ethical consistency in al-Balad, the path of ease in al-Layl, and the two final destinations in al-Bayyinah.
94sXD9O24Ys.summary: On the last night of the series he takes outcomes as a Quranic theme: every choice leads somewhere, and the Quran insists we own our choices in a world where the rich and connected escape consequences. The end of Ramadan raises the same question as the end of life, and returning to how you were before wastes a month that was meant as a workshop and launching pad. From al-Balad he draws ethical consistency: the steep path is freeing captives and feeding the hungry on a day you yourself are hungry, because a value that disappears in hard times is only a preference. The Prophet, expelled from his own city, never became cruel. Believers keep each other steady by urging patience and compassion, and only two outcomes exist. From al-Layl he explains that givers and the God-conscious are eased toward ease in this life itself, inner ease rather than freedom from hardship, while the stingy are eased toward hardship, so the deal is win-win or lose-lose. Al-Bayyinah names the worst and best of creation by their choices, made against relentless time. The best are with their Lord; mutual satisfaction, seeing Allah's face and the healing of every inner wound await those who revere Him.

outline.heading: Opening
A guest who leaves too quickly
outline.gist: No one knows if they will see another Ramadan; he measures his own life by which Ramadans events fell between, so cherish its final hours.

outline.heading: Outcomes as a Quranic theme
outline.gist: Every choice and path ends in an outcome you are stuck with; the Quran's insistence on owning consequences is refreshing where the rich and connected get bailed out.

outline.heading: What is the outcome of your Ramadan?
outline.gist: The end of the month, of a recitation of the Quran and of a life all ask what comes next; slipping back to how things were wastes thirty days of momentum.

outline.heading: Ramadan is the workshop, not the outcome
outline.gist: Ramadan is where you push and strive so that the outcome, in a long life or after death, is good.

outline.heading: Interlude
90:11-16: the steep path of ethical consistency
outline.gist: Free the captive and feed an orphan relative or a destitute person on a day you are hungry yourself: generosity that stops when times are hard was never a value.

outline.heading: A value is always there
outline.gist: Rich or poor, a real ethic defines your character; al-Balad came as the Prophet was being driven from the city of his forefathers back to Ibrahim.

outline.heading: Expelled but never embittered
outline.gist: Being driven from his city did not make the Prophet cruel, rude or hateful; he had climbed that obstacle long before and stayed who he was meant to be.

outline.heading: 90:17-18: urging patience and compassion
outline.gist: Believers remind each other when one loses perseverance or grows harsh; that mutual advice keeps the values alive and puts them among the people of the right.

outline.heading: 90:19-20: the people of the ill omen
outline.gist: Those who rejected the signs, who called prophets a bad omen, face a fire closed over them; there are only two outcomes and no third way.

outline.heading: Keep advising one another
outline.gist: Without mutual reminders to patience and compassion we lose our principles, then the deen, and then all sense of right and wrong.

outline.heading: 92:4-7: diverse paths, one common core
outline.gist: Everyone's striving differs, and that is fine, but all must share giving, God-consciousness and affirming the best that was revealed.

outline.heading: Eased toward ease or toward hardship
outline.gist: Al-yusra here is a way of life, Islam itself, not only Paradise; the stingy and self-sufficient are eased toward the hardest life.

outline.heading: Win-win or lose-lose
outline.gist: Had Allah offered a bad life now for Paradise later, people would weigh the trade; instead the right choice brings ease now and the best outcome later.

outline.heading: Ease is inside the heart
outline.gist: Not freedom from illness or poverty, but inner ease; wealth and health mean nothing without love, a good family and sleep with a clear conscience.

outline.heading: Interlude
Follow Muhammad and find ease
outline.gist: He addresses the young: Islam is the best way to live; ask those who lived with Allah whether they found it hard.

outline.heading: Companions who left with nothing, content
outline.gist: Many died with no inheritance yet fully satisfied; even a few nights of Ramadan gave you a taste of that inner peace.

outline.heading: Fasting to feed the spirit
outline.gist: Set the body aside for a month and nurture the spirit, and you find something that outweighs life's sorrow; the Quran recited all month is that ease.

outline.heading: 98:6: the worst of creatures by their own choice
outline.gist: Disbelievers among the People of the Book and the pagans are called the worst of creation because they had a choice that could have led elsewhere.

outline.heading: Time has no mercy
outline.gist: You hold your destiny; preoccupation with legacy and wealth leaves no time for what comes next, and time marches on without pause, so decide now.

outline.heading: 98:7-8: 'with their Lord' is enough
outline.gist: The best of creation made hard right choices; his teacher said the words 'with their Lord' suffice, everything after is an extra.

outline.heading: Rivers flowing beneath: self-sufficient gardens
outline.gist: Land watered from someone else's territory lives in fear of a dam upstream; Paradise's rivers run beneath its gardens so nothing can be cut off.

outline.heading: Mutual satisfaction
outline.gist: Allah is pleased with them and they with Him; he introduces the narration in Ahmad about the most pampered person on earth.

outline.heading: The most pampered, dipped in the Fire
outline.gist: A single dip in Hell makes the most comfortable person ever to live forget he ever knew a good day.

outline.heading: You are more blessed than you think
outline.gist: Sitting in the masjid on the 29th night, among Muslims, with the Quran, you have more than you could hope for.

outline.heading: The most miserable, dipped in Paradise
outline.gist: Someone abused, sick and poor all his life forgets every pain after one dip in Paradise.

outline.heading: The highest rank: seeing His face
outline.gist: Even the last to enter Paradise receives a kingdom many times the earth; the highest see their Lord's face twice a day and spend the time between waiting for it.

outline.heading: The source of all beauty
outline.gist: Nothing in Paradise is more beloved than seeing Allah, because He is the source of every created beauty there.

outline.heading: Forgotten in a hundred years
outline.gist: Nothing you own will last and even descendants rarely remember grandparents; only what you did remains as the outcome of a life.

outline.heading: Satisfaction that heals every wound
outline.gist: Allah keeps giving until the hunger, mistreatment and trauma no therapy could reach are gone and nothing inside can hurt you again.

outline.heading: For those who revere their Lord
outline.gist: Khashyah blends love, fear of just punishment and respect; this reward is for those who know Allah and revere Him.

outline.heading: Outro
The last night is still open
outline.gist: Even if the month went by with little done, Allah can still draw you in with those He accepted; take your weakness and struggles to Him and no one else.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Accountability before Allah and goals
themes.note: Every choice has an outcome you own; the worst and best of creation are defined by choices made against relentless time.

themes.label: Ramadan: preparation, fasting, making the most of it
themes.note: Ramadan is a workshop and launching pad; going back to old habits wastes its momentum.

themes.label: Values, principles and ethics as a system
themes.note: A value must be consistent in good times and bad, as the expelled Prophet's character stayed unchanged.

themes.label: Zakat, charity and giving
themes.note: The steep path is freeing captives and feeding the needy even when you are hungry yourself.

themes.label: Brotherhood, companionship and friendship
themes.note: Believers keep each other steady by urging patience and compassion whenever one slips.

themes.label: Contentment and acceptance (ridha)
themes.note: The ease promised in al-Layl is inner ease in this life, which the companions had despite owning nothing.

themes.label: Time, opportunity and seizing the moment
themes.note: Time is merciless and never slows, so the choice must be made now.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: Paradise's self-sustaining gardens, mutual satisfaction, the dips in Fire and Paradise and the vision of Allah.

themes.label: Knowing Allah / relationship with Allah
themes.note: Seeing Allah is the highest joy because He is the source of all beauty.

themes.label: Mental health, anxiety and emotional wellbeing
themes.note: Allah's final gift heals the trauma and pain people carry and cannot articulate.

hadith.gist: Allah moves the soil of Paradise and water springs out wherever He wishes.
The most pampered person of the world is dipped once in Hell and says he never saw any good; the most miserable is dipped once in Paradise and says he never knew any hardship.
The last person to enter Paradise receives a kingdom many times the size of the earth; the highest ranks see the face of their Lord morning and evening.

maxims: Ramadan is the workshop, not the outcome
It's not a value if it's not consistent
Islam is the ultimate ease
It's win-win or lose-lose
Time has no rahma
I know my life through Ramadan

stories.who: The Prophet expelled from Makkah
stories.point: Being driven out did not change his character; real values hold under any circumstances.

stories.who: Companions who died without inheritance
stories.point: They left content and wanting only more closeness to Allah, proof of the inner ease Islam brings.

stories.who: His teacher on 'with their Lord'
stories.point: Being with Allah is the whole reward; everything else is an extra.

contemporary: The wealthy and well-connected being bailed out of consequences
Upstream dams that can cut off a downstream country's water, as on the Nile
takeaways: Do not slip back to your pre-Ramadan self; treat the month as a launching pad.
Keep your generosity and other values constant whether times are good or hard.
Remind those around you to be patient and compassionate, and accept their reminders.
Make your choices now, knowing time will not wait and each one shapes your outcome.
Take your weaknesses and struggles to Allah on the last night and keep asking for the outcome you hope for.

tlseapPw7MQ.speaker: adnan
tlseapPw7MQ.speaker_note: continues his own values series, uses a Syrian expression and refers to yesterday's talk
tlseapPw7MQ.title: The Values of Islam: Nobility and Generosity (Muru'ah and Karam)
tlseapPw7MQ.one_line: Muru'ah, the fulfilment of one's humanity, and generosity are high ideals Muslims must revive once the basic ethics are secure.
tlseapPw7MQ.summary: Continuing the week of high ideals, he stresses that values such as forgiveness, nobility and generosity are not obligations one is punished for neglecting, but they flourish only where the non-negotiable basics of justice and righteousness are secure. He explains muru'ah, rooted in the Arabic word for a human being, as reaching the full potential of humanity: doing whatever adorns character and avoiding whatever dents it. Pre-Islamic Arabs prized it, competing to be the one who says 'leave it to me' when someone is in need, and Islam simply purified the intention. Khadijah's description of the Prophet carrying the burdens of others shows he lived this before and after revelation, and hadith critics would reject a narrator whose conduct lacked muru'ah even if nothing he did was unlawful. His favourite story is of Uthman ibn Talhah, not yet Muslim, escorting Umm Salamah hundreds of kilometres to Madinah with complete propriety and never mentioning it. On generosity he contrasts Hatim's fame with the Prophet's generosity and Abu Bakr's giving away all he had, ending with a story of Abu Bakr giving even his clothes to the poor. He calls for these ideals to be revived in homes and in raising children.

outline.heading: Opening
High ideals protected by basic ethics
outline.gist: This week's values are ideals that become possible only once justice and righteousness are solid in a society.

outline.heading: Why the ideals came last
outline.gist: Presenting them first would mislead; forgiveness is not obligatory, but the basic ethics are non-negotiable maxims of the deen.

outline.heading: Muru'ah: the pinnacle of humanity
outline.gist: From the root for a human being, muru'ah is realizing humanity's potential, prized by the Arabs, and defined as doing what adorns character and avoiding what dents it.

outline.heading: Leave it to me: the moment of muru'ah
outline.gist: The Arabs sought chances to take on someone's problem publicly; Islam kept this and purified the intention.

outline.heading: The Prophet's muru'ah before revelation
outline.gist: Khadijah reassured him that Allah would never disgrace one who carries the weak and gives to the needy.

outline.heading: Muru'ah in judging hadith narrators
outline.gist: A narrator could be rejected for dishonourable conduct such as stinginess even if nothing he did was unlawful.

outline.heading: Uthman ibn Talhah escorts Umm Salamah
outline.gist: After her family separated her from her husband and son, a non-Muslim from Makkah escorted her to Madinah with complete propriety and never spoke of it.

outline.heading: Generosity: Hatim, the Prophet and Abu Bakr
outline.gist: Generosity is half of muru'ah; the Prophet was more generous than the rain-bearing wind and Abu Bakr gave all his wealth.

outline.heading: Beyond zakat: a generous society
outline.gist: Zakat is the obligation, but the ideal is a society that enjoys giving, which injustice makes impossible.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr gives away his caravan and his clothes
outline.gist: Finding Madinah in need, he gave away a whole caravan and then his clothing, arriving at the Prophet's gathering in a wheat sack.

outline.heading: Is he pleased with his Lord?
outline.gist: He was told Allah was pleased with him and asked if he was pleased with his Lord, and wept; he later regained wealth.

outline.heading: Bring these ideals back home
outline.gist: Children must be raised to be generous and noble, or Muslims will remain far from what they once were.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Muru'ah: nobility, dignity and chivalry
themes.note: Muru'ah is the full realization of humanity, shown by the Prophet and by a non-Muslim's noble escort of Umm Salamah.

themes.label: Zakat, charity and giving
themes.note: Generosity beyond zakat is an ideal, modelled by the Prophet and Abu Bakr.

themes.label: Values, principles and ethics as a system
themes.note: High ideals are optional but depend on the obligatory basic ethics being secure.

themes.label: The companions and the early generations
themes.note: Abu Bakr's total generosity and Allah's pleasure with him.

themes.label: Seeking knowledge, learning and scholars
themes.note: Hadith critics weighed a narrator's honour and conduct, not only his memory.

themes.label: Parenting and raising children
themes.note: Generosity and nobility must be cultivated in children at home.

hadith.gist: Khadijah: Allah will never disgrace you; you keep ties of kinship, carry the burdens of the weak, give to the destitute and help in hardship
The Prophet was the most generous of people, more generous than the free-blowing wind
Abu Bakr brought all his wealth and, asked what he left for his family, said Allah and His Messenger
Abu Bakr, dressed in a rough garment after giving everything, was told Allah is pleased with him and asked whether he was pleased with his Lord

maxims: Muru'ah is being truly human
Do what adorns character; leave what dents it
Half of muru'ah is generosity
Islam only purified the intention

stories.who: Uthman ibn Talhah and Umm Salamah
stories.point: True nobility protects the vulnerable at personal cost and never boasts of it.

stories.who: Khadijah reassuring the Prophet
stories.point: The Prophet's life was defined by carrying others' burdens even before revelation.

stories.who: Abu Bakr's caravan and wheat sack
stories.point: Generosity so complete that he gave his own clothes, and Allah's pleasure with him.

stories.who: Hatim al-Ta'i
stories.point: Arab generosity was celebrated, and many matched Hatim.

contemporary: Remnants of Arab hospitality that still survive today
takeaways: Be the person who says 'leave it to me' when someone needs help, for Allah's sake
Avoid conduct that dents your dignity even when it is not unlawful
Give beyond zakat and learn to enjoy giving
Raise children to be generous and noble
Secure justice in the community so these ideals can flourish

2:102.en: And they followed [instead] what the devils had recited during the reign of Solomon. It was not Solomon who disbelieved, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic and that which was revealed to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. But the two angels do not teach anyone unless they say, "We are a trial, so do not disbelieve [by practicing magic]." And [yet] they learn from them that by which they cause separation between a man and his wife. But they do not harm anyone through it except by permission of Allah. And the people learn what harms them and does not benefit them. But the Children of Israel certainly knew that whoever purchased the magic would not have in the Hereafter any share. And wretched is that for which they sold themselves, if they only knew

uexim-XLSTw.title: The Philosophy of Islamic Thought #6: Psychology, Physical Health and the Lifestyle of Wellness in Islam
uexim-XLSTw.one_line: Islam's layered model of the human self, its ethic of the body as a trust, and a balanced lifestyle, with cautions on jinn, magic and mental illness.
uexim-XLSTw.summary: He opens by explaining that young Muslims doing dawah must argue from root principles, such as a theory of human nature, rather than from isolated stories, and that faith should never be built on or lost over tertiary narrations. Islam sees the human being as layered: body, spirit, soul, intellect, conscience and subconscious, each named in the Quran, so it offers a real psychological model rather than mystical poetry. The subconscious absorbs everything poured into it, so garbage in means garbage out. Humans are morally responsible, mind, body and spirit affect one another, and discipline can reshape character. Tazkiyah is a third of the din. Human nature cannot be changed, only behaviour, which explains rules on seclusion and safeguarding property; Islam embraces nature and channels it rather than repressing it. The nafs is a loving but ignorant cheerleader that can be tamed in stages, while Shaytan is weak but unpersuadable. The body is a trust: no self-harm, no excess or ascetic neglect, value strength and eat lightly. A well lifestyle has prayer as a structured pause, moderate eating, disciplined sleep, community and service. He firmly rejects jinn possession and present-day black magic as explanations for illness, insists ruqya never replaces professional care, and says mental illness is not a sign of weak iman.

outline.heading: Why this series: dawah at the ideological level
outline.gist: Non-Muslims steeped in other philosophies ask what Islam's theory of knowledge, ethics and economics are, and Muslims must answer at that level.

outline.heading: Young Muslims will be sized up by ideologues
outline.gist: Older believers may not need this, but students facing atheists, liberals or Marxists must explain the principles behind the examples.

outline.heading: Argue from root principles, not end rulings
outline.gist: On modesty or polygamy, ask what in the moral system or view of human nature someone actually disputes.

outline.heading: Do not build or lose faith on tertiary stories
outline.gist: A narration in Bukhari should not shake your iman; faith rests on the big framework questions, not on doubt websites.

outline.heading: The architecture of the self: the atheist view
outline.gist: Materialism sees a person as the sum of evolution, synapses and environment with no further layer.

outline.heading: Not a mind trapped in a disposable body
outline.gist: The mind can imagine what the body never can, as with Star Wars, but Islam sees a layered creature rather than a floating mind.

outline.heading: The layers named: body, spirit, soul, intellect, conscience, subconscious
outline.gist: The Quran distinguishes them clearly; modern psychology also speaks of a self beyond the ego, and Allah breathing His spirit into us signals an intimate bond.

outline.heading: When one layer is sick: the heart and the subconscious
outline.gist: Everything seen, heard and suffered pours into the subconscious; feed it haram and you get haram out.

outline.heading: A psychological model, not mystical poetry
outline.gist: Islam's model parallels exposure in modern psychology and deserves recognition as a competing, often superior model.

outline.heading: Assumption one: humans are morally responsible
outline.gist: We do not prosecute a pet lion; Western thought wants moral responsibility without the metaphysics that generates it.

outline.heading: Assumption two: mind, body and spirit affect each other
outline.gist: Accountability requires mental soundness and functioning senses, which is why the born deaf-blind are not held accountable.

outline.heading: Assumption three: discipline and reflection reshape character
outline.gist: How you are need not be how you stay; the model is closer to virtue ethics than reductionist neurochemistry, without denying biology.

outline.heading: Tazkiyah as a third of the din
outline.gist: Practice, belief and inner purification; morality fails without constant self-questioning about motives like vanity, anger or selfishness.

outline.heading: Taking the best of revelation and the mystery of the spirit
outline.gist: Self-purification lets you use texts in their best way; the spirit remains a matter of Allah's command.

outline.heading: Human nature cannot change, behaviour can
outline.gist: Men are men and women have natures too; two people left on an island will pair up, so Islam regulates behaviour such as seclusion.

outline.heading: Unattended wealth teaches theft
outline.gist: A Syrian proverb and the requirement that stolen property was properly secured both acknowledge human nature.

outline.heading: Islam embraces human nature rather than repressing it
outline.gist: No shame in what you feel; desires are expressed through healthy, regulated channels, and vows of celibacy are not accepted.

outline.heading: The nafs: your loving but ignorant cheerleader
outline.gist: Born where spirit met body, it wants survival, food, mating and dominance; not evil, it can be taught over time.

outline.heading: Shaytan: weaker but unpersuadable
outline.gist: Unlike the nafs he cannot be influenced, but he has little real power.

outline.heading: Stages of taming the nafs and the thought-action-emotion cycle
outline.gist: From submission to struggle, coercion, acceptance and love; changing thoughts and actions eventually changes feelings.

outline.heading: Modern therapy echoes the Prophetic model
outline.gist: A psychiatrist tells a depressed patient to wake, dress and walk daily; behaviour change reshapes the mind.

outline.heading: The body as a trust: five principles
outline.gist: No self-harm, no excess in activity or idleness, strength is valued, prevention beats cure and overconsumption is discouraged.

outline.heading: Against ascetic neglect of the body
outline.gist: Early ascetics starved themselves; Ali drank cold water because it draws deeper gratitude.

outline.heading: Fasting as metabolic discipline
outline.gist: The body is entrusted, so no tattoos or mutilation; Ramadan recalibrates appetite and metabolism rather than starving.

outline.heading: Prayer as embodied devotion and hygiene as faith
outline.gist: Each posture carries a spiritual meaning, and cleanliness is part of the din itself.

outline.heading: The least followed hadith: the stomach
outline.gist: No vessel is worse to fill than the stomach; leave a third for breath, consume less so you are healthier and the planet suffers less.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: write down your schedule
outline.gist: When someone cannot memorize Quran he has them write and stare at their day; moderation is the principle.

outline.heading: Spiritual rhythm: prayer as a structured pause
outline.gist: Each prayer is a time-out that resets you amid the day's stimuli and leads to better decisions.

outline.heading: Nutritional moderation
outline.gist: Overconsumption is corrosive physically and spiritually; enjoy meals but be reasonable.

outline.heading: Sleep discipline
outline.gist: The Prophet never stayed up a full night outside battle; eating more makes you sleep more, and students should be asleep before midnight on weekdays.

outline.heading: Afiyah: wellbeing of body, mind and spirit
outline.gist: Wellbeing is the best gift; maintain it in every dimension.

outline.heading: Community health: isolation is spiritually risky
outline.gist: Solitude for reflection is good but loneliness is not; congregational worship and visiting the sick keep people connected.

outline.heading: Service heals
outline.gist: Studies now confirm altruism improves wellbeing; healing another suffering soul heals your own.

outline.heading: The feedback loop and why balance is harder than extremism
outline.gist: Sin disturbs the heart, which unsettles the psyche, the body and spiritual discipline; break the cycle anywhere and keep calibrating.

outline.heading: Jinn cannot hijack the psyche
outline.gist: Exorcisms are baseless and harmful; telling a paranoid patient a jinn is inside him plants a belief no medication can remove.

outline.heading: Black magic as superstition today
outline.gist: Marital breakdowns come from ego and incompatibility, not a paper hidden with goat hair.

outline.heading: Envy and the evil eye are real but not a diagnosis
outline.gist: Take the protective steps, but look for real causes so you can change outcomes.

outline.heading: Tailored rulings for OCD, anxiety and depression
outline.gist: People with mental illness need personal guidance, and some tazkiyah practices like humility talks can harm the self-loathing.

outline.heading: Ruqya is not a substitute for care
outline.gist: Recite over loved ones daily, but just as ruqya does not set a fracture, it does not replace professional treatment.

outline.heading: Mental illness is not weak iman
outline.gist: Blaming weak faith deprives people of simple treatment; strong iman helps manage illness but does not replace care.

outline.heading: Wellness as Islam in action
outline.gist: Values become concrete in how the Prophet slept, ate, walked and spoke.

outline.heading: Q&A: stages or departments of the nafs
outline.gist: The nafs commanding evil is the same self being tamed; the more connected the conscience is to Allah, the more it reproaches the self.

takeaways: Base your faith and your dawah on the big framework questions, not isolated stories
Guard what enters your subconscious through eyes, ears and company
Treat your body as a trust: eat less, sleep before midnight, stay active and clean
Use the daily prayers as pauses to reset, and stay connected to community and service
Seek professional help for mental illness; ruqya and iman support it but do not replace it
